That was when different methods were used. Muslims who were left without jobs were designated to clean the streets and do the worst menial jobs, and it was done in such a way that Muslim intellectuals were designated to do such jobs. For instance, the deputy chief of police, who was a Muslim, doctors were designated to work on the marketplace, and this was a way of creating an atmosphere that will be conducive to people leaving. If you have an intellectual cleaning, sweeping streets, what can then an ordinary Muslim who does not enjoy any protection expect? And that was when the Muslims themselves asked to be allowed to move out because they had no other alternative. They were afraid of being taken to the Batkovic camp or of being driven out in some worse manner. And that was the origin of this petition. It was a pressure simply exerted in a different manner but conducing the Muslims or, rather, compelling them to leave without any choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was my understanding that Muslims were brought to a very unfavourable and difficult condition, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you may put questions to the witness. In relation to the last document of which the witness said that he hasn't seen it before, he has heard about such a document. It will be returned to you. If you want to tender that, we will hear whether there would be any objection once it has been translated. The answers given by the witness are understandable, as well, without having a specific look at this document, but you still have an opportunity to tender that document at a later stage if you have any wish to do so. The witness testified about a petition he heard of that was sent to the Red Cross. Your last question, you said, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I am sorry for having to ask you this: When you were young, just as your son is, were you ever assigned custodianship, guardianship?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I don't see the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik -- we'll first ask the witness to take his earphones off. Would you tell us what the relevance is?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you can. I have to apologise for this. Let me call it stupidity. That is the clearest way of expressing myself. It would be your last question anyhow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the worst thing that could happen is that an irrelevant question would be put to the witness. To have it all sorted out would take us five to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My only concern is that given the nature of what it might be and if it turns out to be irrelevant and shouldn't be asked, maybe it should be done in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, then, if that would be a solution, Mr. Krajisnik, in order to protect the witness on the one-hand side, on the other to allow you to put to the witness what you'd like to, I suggest that we turn to private session. I see you nodding yes. We turn to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber wonders whether it makes any sense to start in between the next witness or whether we would give you, Mr. Hannis -- how much time do you think you need? Thirty-five minutes, would that do? I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was going to ask for 30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's, then, have a beak for 30 minutes, and we start, then, at twenty minutes past five. We'll see if any time remains to start the next witness. It, of course, depends on the time you need, Mr. Hannis, and the time the Chamber would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Twenty-five past is 25 minutes. I don't know -- I don't know how long Mr. Hannis is really going to have if he's giving away that five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I offered 35 minutes. He asked for 30 minutes, and then I said we would have a break until twenty-five minutes past five.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I thought Your Honour was intending to give him 30. That was -- I apologise for the intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now could I just have until 5.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can have until 5.30, and I'll re-read the transcript later on to see how time is calculated in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I address something before we have the witness come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to give you an opportunity to do so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to address some of the documents that were given to me in relation to questions that counsel asked on cross-examine. First I want to address one that Mr. Krajisnik used to ask a question in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In conversation with my language assistant, this appears to be a document from the police station in Lopare, where Mr. Davidovic grew up. It appears to refer to something when he was age 17, and it appears to be a notation in the records of the police department that he was referred or his parents were counselled to exercise stricter supervision over him. I don't know more details than that. I do note that the fax date on this is the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it give any reason specifically? Was it because --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I can't read the B/C/S, but in my interpretation it didn't appear to refer to a specific incident. I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My concern is, Your Honour, we've gone into private session now, and, of course, that was at my request. But first of all, I don't see how this is relevant, but we've gone into private session, and the public may have a perception that ah, there was some deep dark secret about Mr. Davidovic when this was the kind of thing that -- I don't know in your jurisdiction, Your Honour, in mine, a juvenile record not amounting to any kind of conviction would have been destroyed years ago. It has no -- it just has no relevance or no bearing. I would like, when we go back into public session, if somehow we can address it if you agree that it has any relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first -- okay. That's one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a related comment to that, Your Honour, this was faxed on the 8th of June. If this is something that is shared with us ahead of time we can have discussions with counsel about whether or not this would be appropriate to bring to court and spend court time on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least, whatever has been said about this first document is now being repeated not in private session, but I don't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think it's really a big problem. I would almost say that all boys stand who never have visited a police office. I could not stand up at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just in relation to that last comment from Mr. Hannis and a related comment to that, Your Honour, this was faxed on the 8th June. If this is something that is shared with us ahead of time, we can have discussions with counsel about whether this would be appropriate to bring to court and spend court time on. Your Honour, I didn't cross-examine on it. I did not think it was appropriate to spend court time on it. That's why there was no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. There is no need, at this moment, to take distance from it, but I do understand from what Mr. Hannis said that it's mainly addressing Mr. Krajisnik that -- one thing is for sure, Mr. Krajisnik, whenever you want to introduce any documents, let me be quite clear on that, if it is in evidence you should give the number under which it is admitted into evidence. If you have any difficulties in identifying that number, please seek the help needed. That should be possible. Secondly, give a list of all documents prior to putting it to any witness to Madam Registrar so that she can try to find out, to retrieve that document so it can be used without any further problems. If there is such a document as we're discussing at this moment, you should consult with counsel before you introduce such a document. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Among the other documents I received during the first break that were to be the basis for some of the questions that counsel asked, one of them is what appears to be a criminal report from an individual, a private citizen. There's an individual named that does not appear to be from the MUP, but it's sent to the public prosecutor, and it appears, if I can read the date, maybe June of 2004, complaining about some alleged conduct of Mr. Davidovic. There is no criminal complaint. There's no document from the court or from the public prosecutor. So if this was the basis for asking the question about whether there's a criminal complaint against him, I would submit it's inadequate. I don't know how it was transmitted between counsel and the client because I know it's in B/C/S, so it wasn't read, but, Your Honour, it does not, I think, support the question that was asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, any question on the last observation by Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It wasn't put forward as the -- that document was not put forward as the basis. I supplied with -- Mr. Hannis with the documentation that I had, but that particular document was not put forward as the basis for the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any stronger basis for that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. That's information that was received by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But has this been substantiated in any kind of document or, from -- I mean, on a documentary basis is there any stronger basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I provided Mr. Hannis with a whole series of documents. If Mr. Hannis wants to go through them with the Court, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. And in answer to your question, this appears to be the strongest one in regard to any criminal complaint. The next one is a document that appears to be a civil appeal regarding a complaint against Mr. Davidovic's company, his business, not in an individual capacity. On -- he prevailed in the lower level, I understand from the language assistant. However, on appeal it was partially reversed, and he was ordered to pay -- his company was ordered to pay some damages. So that was a civil proceeding. And this second one -- this next one is also a civil judgement against his company for money damages. The third one is a document from June 30, 1992, signed by him, which appears to be from the Bijeljina CSB, the regional police centre, in which it documents that a vehicle was inspected and determined to be appropriate for use by the MUP. I suppose this was a document that was relied on to support the question about seizing documents -- seizing vehicles for his personal use, but it's an official -- it appears to be an official MUP document. The next one is the same regarding inspection of a vehicle. And the last item appears to be something from the local cadaster reflecting the sale of land from Mr. Davidovic to a private individual, a woman, on the 21st of March, 2005. And those are the only documents I received. And, again, that reflects my concern, Your Honour, about these things, if they had them ten days or two weeks ahead of time, we would request we'd be provided, we can discuss -- it doesn't appear to support the kinds of questions that were asked and the impression that's given about Mr. Davidovic, and that troubles me greatly, Your Honour. I think we need to change the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand your complaint to be that this is approaching a witness in a harassing and intimidating way on insufficient grounds. Before the Chamber can form its opinion on it, of course, we would need to inspect all these documents after they have been translated. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if we're in closed session or in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're in open session, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that was interpreted by the Prosecutor was not explained fully. Under the legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, and the former Yugoslavia, the criminal offences do not have a statute of limitations applying to them. It's different for the traffic violations. So this was an offence. We don't know its origins, but it remains on the file. And this was something that had to do with both the parents and the guardians and their supervision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're commenting on the document. We'll see once the document is translated, whether it formed a sufficient basis for putting the questions on what a witness is supposed to have done when he was 17. Mr. Hannis, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- call the witness for redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom, or Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, I just want to make a comment, if I may, in relation to Mr. Hannis' comments, and I can probably make them at the end of the evidence of this particular witness because I see he's about to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's entering the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we move the ELMO slightly so I could see the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, I want to ask you about some of the questions you were asked on cross-examination, and I'm going to go to page 14 -- 14362, at line 15. Ms. Loukas was asking you about a meeting you told us about in April or May at Bosanksa Veija [phoen], where you mentioned Mr. Krajisnik was on the premises. Can you tell us first of all what was Bosanksa Veija? Was that a hotel? Was that a building? What was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war in the former Yugoslavia, every republic had its own venue where the highest officials would meet, and that's what Bosnia- Herzegovina had, was called Bijela Veija, and that's where the high officials could meet and discuss matters that needed to be discussed. They even had bedrooms there. With the start of the war, this villa was given for use to the Serb leadership, and they used it for these purposes until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This meeting that you described, can you tell us how you came to be there? How did you know there was going to be a meeting? Were you invited? How did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Stanisic invited me to that meeting, and the point was that we should meet and discuss how we were to go about the transport of ammunition and so on and so forth because he knew I was going to be involved in that. I saw him there; that is Mico. I saw Arkan there and Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who did you talk with? Did you talk with anyone other than Mico Stanisic while you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Frenki Simatovic there, as well. Arkan was there, and I believe that someone else was there. Once Mr. Krajisnik left the premises and then re-entered with another person. Karadzic came and went twice; he was standing there for a while talking to some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During this discussion was there a sit-down meeting among a group of people, or was this only you talking with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were sitting at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "we," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was I, Mr. Frenki, Mico Stanisic, and Arkan came in later and joined us, and he was in the company of another man who I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. At page 14385, lines 7 and 8, Ms. Loukas asked you about whether you had a copy your report about Edin Hujdurovic, and you said you would check. Were you able to check and see if you have that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have a copy. I have some other documents, and I wanted to ask the Trial Chamber at the end of my testimony whether I should give the documents to them because I didn't not have the opportunity of contacting you. So if you would wish me to I could hand the documents over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you bring them with you when you returned to The Hague for this visit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the documentation with me. I don't know if I have everything, but I do have documents here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll address that with the Court and counsel at the end. At page 14391, beginning with line 1, Ms. Loukas asked you about the document signed by Mr. Krajisnik that Vojkan Dukovic showed you as his authorisation to handle humanitarian resettlement. And she put it to you that there was not any such document, and you said in your answer, "Yes, of course, I can confirm, and I can add further details if you're interested." Can you tell us what further details you can add about that document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was asked about how -- I asked about how it was possible that he had such authorisation and I saw that there was president of the Assembly in the upper left-hand corner. I saw him in the signature, as well. That's why I can state with certainty that it was him. Second, when I wanted to take the document off him, I was wearing civilian clothes at the time and I was unable to compel him to hand the document over, so he put it away somewhere. In the past ten days that I spent at home now, I was contacted by some people who said that they had seen the document. If you want me to I can give you the names of these people. They even told me the details of him showing them the document, if that's interesting to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Could you tell us those names?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lejla Pasic, Edib Hujdurovic. He even held the document in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the same Edib that you helped?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Davidovic, I want to go to page 14405, beginning at line 10. Ms. Loukas had asked you a series of questions about your unit and -- and you regarding certain people and asking whether you had led these people away from their homes. In particular, at this point she was asking you about Husein Apaka, and you said at lines 11 and 12 you were at the corps command when a military officer complained and demanded that Husein be sent to Batkovic for having said something insulting. First of all, can you tell me who was the corps commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander at the time was Mr. Ilic; I don't know his first name. I believe there was a lieutenant colonel or a colonel who showed up and complained of having been intercepted by some people on his way to work, and they were threatening him, or at least that's how that particular officer perceived them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this lieutenant colonel who complained, you didn't know his name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Further on, on that page at line 16, you mention that you regret not having warned Husein. You said, "If I had done so, I would have lost my head." Can you explain to the Judges why or how that would have happened and by whom that would have happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they known that I was unable physically to leave the premises and go over to tell him to go in hiding, I would probably be targeted by them. They usually either mobilised people or threw a hand grenade on their house; who knows what could have happened later on. I did suffer some problems at a later stage, but I don't want to go into details now and tell you how serious they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you relate those later problems to -- well, to what conduct of yours do you relate those later problems?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events in 1992 when we had prevented those attempts at taking people away, they started threatening me, and I'm referring to the people who were around the SDS. I mean, Predrag Zuco, Drago Vukovic, Ljubisa Mauzer, Vojkan, and all the other ones who were guilty of that conduct in Bijeljina, and they were very close to the SDS. There were many who were exposed to their brutal conduct; they even came to search my house during the war. My parents were there, and they were even -- their life was threatened unless they went along with their requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, finally I want to ask you a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple questions to finish up, Mr. Davidovic. Defence counsel asked you a number of questions and suggested or insinuated that you engaged in various activity that might have amounted to criminal activity or near-criminal activity. You denied all those, as I understand your testimony. Who would have a motive to make up those kinds of things about you?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. There is no basis for that sort of question; it's speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if you ask the witness whether he is aware of anyone who has a motive or whether he ever formed an opinion on certain events that could have created a motive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, because it's your position that those allegations are untrue and assuming that's the case, do you have any experience that would lead you to have reached a conclusion about who would make up things like that about you? First just say yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you'll allow me, I, in fact, wanted to tell you more about it. During the war, while I was working for the police and as a member of the police doing my best to prevent such unlawful conduct, I would end up in a situation where I had to protect myself and my family. Sometimes I could not even go to Bijeljina. I must admit that the times were very difficult because people would be killed or go missing overnight and then be found dead somewhere. All this was happening simply because that's the sort of people that were in power, and one could not do anything about it. When I returned from my earlier testimony here, everybody knew that I was a witness before this Tribunal, and they reported it on the TV as if I had been accusing some people. The local newspaper wrote about me being a criminal. I was never, ever standing trial. I had a labour dispute going on, but that was related to my company, and I was never in a situation that would end up in any criminal complaints. I did my job professionally as a police officer. But what I wanted to say is that in the last ten days, those persons who I have been mentioning in my testimony were visited by people who wanted them to sign statements to the effect that this was not true and that they should conjure allegations against me. I wish to remind you that the SDS is still in power there, that they have the police force under their control and all the other institutions. And I can tell you that it isn't easy to testify here and withstand all the pressure that I have been exposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other matter that I want to address is, I think, with counsel I have discussed -- there was an issue regarding whether Mr. Krajisnik was in New York for negotiations. Mr. Davidovic had said 1991 and 1992 in his statement. We have in Mr. Okun's diary, there is a reference in, I think, in Exhibit 212 --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no contest that Mr. Krajisnik was in New York in 1993. He just wasn't in New York late 1991, early 1992 as indicated by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have an agreement with counsel that Mr. Krajisnik was in New York in March of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I think that's what I just said, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas. Let me first see.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just was asking if the Bench had any questions. I apologise. Judge Hanoteau has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as part of the missions you accomplished in Sarajevo, in Bijeljina, in Brcko, and in Zvornik, I would like to know whether you had the feeling that you were in a position to accomplish these tasks without meeting any obstacles, without meeting any specific obstruction.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think I would have difficulties -- well, I did think I would have difficulties, but I got through the work in about a month. I knew I wouldn't be able to complete the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went there, I was conscious of the fact that what I had to do I wouldn't be able to do without coming across resistance and difficulties, but I was conscious that I would be doing my assignment and that this would contribute to the fact that when the legitimate authorities would be established, then the authorities would realise that this was done in their interests. But as the time space was short, just a month, there were requests for me to withdraw. So it was only in effect for a brief period of time, not lasting in character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These obstacles, this feeling you had that you were not able to accomplish your task fully, but these obstacles you were able to circumvent them because you explained to us that you were in a position to fully accomplish your mission; you were in a position to arrest people; you were in a position to seize property. You were in a position to accomplish the tasks that had been set out to you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my job energetically and with full responsibility without any compromise at all, and this gave me the right to do what I did, and they weren't able to stand up to me, to oppose me. But my presence there and the job that I was doing gave rise to revolt and resistance, and that is why my presence there for them was completely unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is the following, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sir: Who was supporting you? What was helping you to fulfil your mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had full support from my ministry, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I was responsible to them, in fact, and I must say and recognise that in my whole involvement I had the support of Mico Stanisic. He asked that those paramilitaries be disarmed, and he was in contact with us all the time, and he gave us full support. And the police in Republika Srpska was at my service; they provided reinforcements for me. So I didn't have any resistance in that quarter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the question has been asked previously, but I'd like things to be as clear as possible. How can you identify this resistance, the obstacles you were confronted with? If there was a name to put on these obstacles, on this resistance, what name would that be? Who would it be?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs. They were the ones who were the decisive factors. The Crisis Staff supported, up to a point in time, the fact that these paramilitaries should be disarmed, but they left it up to us to do our job. And as soon as I disarmed the paramilitaries, I was no longer acceptable. And the problem was with those paramilitaries that at one point in time they were set apart from the Crisis Staff and did what they wanted. They didn't listen to the Crisis Staff so that not even the Crisis Staff had full control of them. And when they saw that they were not able to control them anymore, what happened? They went to the SUP. They took over the Ministry of the Interior, the local branch. They took over the documentation that they had, weapons permits and so on. They looked for driving licenses, for vehicles. And they could do what they did. And those were the reasons for which the Crisis Staff -- as soon as we finished with them, they went on doing what they did before. They said, Do your job. Disarm the Red Berets. Go to Bijeljina, finish the job with Mauzer and his group, go to Zvornik, finish the job with the Yellow Wasps, and as soon as you finish on the third day you, Mico, withdraw and the others were come in. That's what it was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, what you're saying without any ambiguity, that those were opposed to the accomplishment of your mission were the Crisis Staffs. Thank you, sir. Second question I'd like to ask you, it's a more technical question. As part of your testimony and in your statement, you mentioned the reserve police forces, and at some point you said that the members of the reserve policemen had increased dramatically. My question is the following: I would like you to tell me, to explain to me what were these police reserve forces. What was the role of these forces as part of the institution of the republic? What were they exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try and be brief. At every local organ, at the level of the republic, pursuant to a decision of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly that a reserve force should be established, and it was established pursuant to an Assembly decision, and the Ministry of the Interior was in charge of seeing that there was a full complement in those forces. And then within the frameworks of Bijeljina, for example, or Tuzla, the centre Tuzla with the 18 municipalities there would be so many members of the reserve force. In Bilje itself, that many. The strength, the force. Now, each local commune within the municipality in Bijeljina, there were 54 local communities in actual fact. In each local commune a reserve police station was established, and it was formed exclusively of members, civilians, persons who had done their military service and who had some basic concepts of handling weapons, for example. And those individuals were then further trained over a longer period of time from '78 or '79 when the reserve force was filled up with members. During the winter months every year they would have several hours of training, and they would be capacitated to be reserve policemen, trained to be reserve policemen. So Bijeljina had a certain number of reserve policemen of that kind. And according to the socialist system and the defence in the socialist system, and each individual was a member of the defence system, that implied that the members of the reserve force should take over the functions of the police force in the local commune itself. Once the war had started -- when the war started, of the number that was there already, let's say 400 men, this number was increased overnight to 1.200 without any decision being made on the part of any organ. Of course, there was probably some body who issued orders to the local SUP to do that. I say that from the aspects of Bijeljina. And all those people who were there, the number was raised, the number of members was raised. Uniforms were supplied. There weren't enough uniforms, so uniforms had to be supplied and weapons too. But this was the reserve force of the police who had their weapons in the MUP organ, and later on the reserve force was expanded. So there were 400 members to begin with and 1.200 afterwards. So this became a military unit which, in fact, carried out assignments pursuant to orders from the authorities in these inter-ethnic conflicts. The police took over the role of being able to do this. Checkpoints were set up; controls were set up. The comings and goings of persons and vehicles was established. I don't know if I have succeeded in explaining this to you, but that's what the organisation was like. That's what happened. And once the elections had taken place, the SDS members would send in members, and the children of those people, they would make up these numbers for a full complement of the reserve force, bring them up to strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you talk about paramilitary groups, do you also include people coming from the reserve police? Those groups of paramilitaries, were they formed from those police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The paramilitaries weren't formed from the reserve police force and the police force. The paramilitaries were formed of individuals who had come in and established separate units. All of them had names of some kind, the Guards or the Sokols, the Eagles, the scorpions, the Red Berets, or whatever. They had people from outside mostly, people who hadn't been in any military formation, people who hadn't done their military service at all. And in each local commune they would collect together on that basis, and they were placed at the function and disposal of the local authorities, and their leaders for the most part were either members of the Crisis Staff or members of the inner circle of SDS leadership. And these paramilitary formations were stronger even than members of the police force. Nobody was able to stand up to them. They had modern weapons, heavy weaponry even. They had APCs, sophisticated weapons. So nobody was able to stand up to them. The regular police forces with their infantry and small arms weren't able to stand up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then those paramilitary groups were just being created spontaneously. Were they being formed under the impulse of an individual, or was there an institution creating them? Was there an institution in place to create, to make sure that such organs were created, such groups were created? Was it spontaneous, or was it organised, and if it was organised, who was behind it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they couldn't have been organised spontaneously. They could volunteer to make up a unit, but there was no spontaneity, that is to say it wasn't on the basis of somebody's will or the will of individuals. Somebody had to supply the weapons to pay for the uniforms, to give them premises, to determine what their assignments were, and they received that from the local Crisis Staffs. Nobody was established as a military, paramilitary information overnight and say I want to take up a weapon and loot. They would be in the function of the local authorities and Crisis Staff, but then they would set up on their own. They would feel themselves to be stronger and more powerful and escape control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again in order to make sure that we understand each other, according to you, nevertheless, those paramilitary groups were formed through the Crisis Staffs. They were the ones who instigated their creation.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each municipality had its own unit. Each place had its own unit, and it didn't want to come under the police or under the army. It was a force apart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one question just to clarify one of your last answers. When you said paramilitary groups were formed through or at the instigation of the Crisis Staffs, were there any paramilitary groups that were already -- you do not hear me, I understand. Do you get translation now? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was some interruption. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard some evidence about Arkan's men or Seselj's men. Were these also paramilitary groups formed through the Crisis Staffs, or were they from a different origin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those paramilitary formations were, in fact, the nucleus of later paramilitary formations. Let me tell you some interesting details. Before Arkan's unit arrived in Bijeljina, they had some training centre on the boarder between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. Now, why did they come to that border belt for training? They waited for an opportune moment to become included into the conflict or to bring the conflict to a head that was looming. So when they arrived, Arkan's men, they didn't dwell on - how shall I put this - on any basics, like who came from outside. Who -- it's the locals that knew that. So they engaged locals from the environment who could tell them who had money, who had property, who had other means and resources, which firms were owned by Croatians and things like that. So when they finished all that and when they came, as they call it -- when they achieved liberty, as they put it, they managed to collect everything that was valuable. For example, the latest vehicle that was bought by the municipality, and this was financed by the citizens, was a vehicle that was looted and taken away from Bijeljina and nobody ever saw it again. So when a group like that was formed, they would get in these -- Savic Ljubisa Mauzer was a result of Arkan's arrival, because after Arkan arrived he would take over local men. So this was all done under the auspices of the Crisis Staff and people from the SDS. There was nobody else. The army was a part; the police was a part. And that is why nobody was able to stand up to them. And when the Crisis Staff felt they were under jeopardy, as they were in Brcko with the red berets arrival, and Crnogorac, he said, Let's disarm those paramilitaries because they're creating problems for us, they actually stood behind them. That's what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Judge Hanoteau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Terribly sorry, sir, but I must ask you another question. I think you said earlier that some Serbs in Bijeljina who did not accept the SDS policies that something happened to them, that some unfortunate things happened to them. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understood me very well. After the SDS came to power, all those who were not in the SDS were replaced overnight; when the armed conflict started in Brcko, for example. Then in Bijeljina they just collected up people who were not SDS members. They would get them out of their houses overnight, mobilise them and send them to the front, which means, We're in power now and you're going to have to fight, and we're here to command. We're here to page policies. So all those who were opposed were mobilised. They were called up, and they were not able to go home from the front line. They were sent to the front, or they would have to gain special permission to go home. They would just round them up off the streets. Many such examples and similar ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Mostly people who were intellectuals, educated people holding responsible positions, respected people, people with authority in the environment in which they lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have the questions of the Bench triggered any need to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have one, Your Honour, because I wasn't sure you got the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic, Judge Orie asked you about your assertion that these paramilitaries were created or formed by the Crisis staffs, and then he asked you about Arkan's men and Seselj's men and, I would add, the Red Berets. Were these created by the Crisis Staffs, or did they have another origin, and if you know, what was that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Red Berets came pursuant to requests by the Crisis Staff; I'm thinking about Brcko. They officially refered to the MUP of Serbia, asking for assistance that the red berets should take part in the front line. Once the red berets arrived they did not report to the army command and be in the -- stand up in the defence of Brcko. They stayed in the town; they took the premises over where they were accommodated; they came over took over command of the SUP, of the police, and did what they did. And the people from the Crisis Staff saw immediately that they had brought in somebody whom didn't suit them, so they said go back. But they didn't want to go back anymore; the Red Berets didn't want to go back anymore. They had -- were in command from Serbia, and they could take over all the goods they wanted to and take them back to Serbia, so it was in their interest to stay on. So nothing could happen without the Crisis Staffs; everything that was done that was authorised by someone. Vojko Djukovic, for example, who rounded up people in Bijeljina, as an example, received the rank of major from Karadzic officially in the town square. He was remunerated for what he did, so nothing was spontaneous; nothing happened at the initiative of an individual or a group without the knowledge or a group of the local powers that be, the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry but I still need to know from you if you know who formed these groups? Who supplied them with weapons and equipment? Who recruited them? How did they get started? Was it the Crisis Staffs or someone or something else, if you know, Arkan's, Seselj's, Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff formed the groups, provided them with weapons and equipment and a building they were to be accommodated with. They supplied them with the initial resources, but as time went on it was citizens who gave in their contributions, people working abroad they would get quite a lot of money on the basis of these contributions to use for uniforms, equipment, their station, and everything else. They had enough weapons, so they didn't actually need weapons, but for everything else, from the dues being paid and coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll stop there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not, however, because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're talking about Red Berets, about Seselj's men, about Arkan's men, when they first were put together as a group, was that done in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or did they come from elsewhere in Bosnia- Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I owe you explanation here when it comes to Bijeljina and the arrival in Bijeljina between Arkan's men and Seselj's groups. There is a big difference there. Arkan's men, Arkan's group had been to Croatia beforehand; they had their trading centre there. They had their barracks there and everything they needed for establishing their unit, whereas when it comes to the radicals or Seselj's mean, in Bijeljina they were not able to do anything and they didn't want to do anything. I have to say that. You see, in Bijeljina the radicals were led by Mirko Blagojevic, who did not have a negative attitude towards the Muslims; quite the contrary. The radicals in Bijeljina led by Mirko Blagojevic led the Muslims; they even issued a proclamation asking that the Muslims be protected and not ethnically cleansed. That's a very interesting piece of information, and the radicals, they were protecting the Muslims. There are a lot of examples to bare this out, where they called for the protection of the Muslims and they asked Mirko Blagojevic for protection. That's very interesting; that's the truth of it that's as it stands. Now, while they themselves were exposed to pleasantness and then they were disbanded, they weren't allowed -- they weren't able to act as a unit, their weapons were confiscated. So -- that is to say, the radicals no longer had any formation, any group, and they had a lot of difficulty in Bijeljina, in actual fact. At the beginning of the war when they became involved and went to Brcko, they were up at the front line there. They went to Brcko, and when they took control of the town, which was a strategic goal at that time, they withdrew to Brcko. They weren't in town looting and taking other people's property and engaging in anything like that. That's the truth of it, and it must be told. The -- now, 12.000 Muslims went to Janja, and the Janja Muslims asked the radicals to protect them. But when it comes to Arkan, he was brought in. He came in from Serbia. He was sent from Serbia; you know how he was sent and they were sent. You heard a lot about that, so you don't need to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You talked about Arkan's men who had been in Croatia. They had their training camps. Who organised the training camps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was organ -- they were organised by the army or, rather, the republican MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By whom were they financed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DAVIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything went via the republican SUP of Serbia; they received their salaries there, their weapons there. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. If there are no further questions from the parties. This concludes your evidence in this court, Mr. Davidovic. I'd like to thank you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for coming, not only once but two times to The Hague and for having answered all the questions. You're excused. Madam Usher, could you please -- or Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Davidovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to offer the exhibits we had in connection with this witness. 764 through 782 were ones that we discussed with him, and then I believe there were another five that we propose as contextual documents, Your Honour. I think it's the --

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, would you be willing to discuss with --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sounds like a sensible arrangement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I suggest that we'll not at this moment go into detail in respect of those documents Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. because they are in a list of documents we still have to consider. In relation to Witness 680, 23rd of June, the Trial Chamber has indicated that it would wait until the list of exhibits including the ones presented by Mr. Krajisnik had been finalised before dealing with admission. Mr. Krajisnik, on these documents you should consult with counsel, and we'd like to invite you to tender those documents into evidence that are not already in evidence within one week from now on. The general rule will be whenever you use any documents in cross-examination you'd like to tender, you'll have to make entirely clear within one week whether you'd like to have them in evidence, and you have to provide the Chamber with English copies of the documents. I further would like to inform you that your cross-examination tends to be more and more time-consuming. We allowed you far beyond what you indicated in respect of this witness. The Chamber might in the near future be more strict on this time. And as I said before, the Defence is invited to agree on how much time would be used by counsel and what time would be needed for remaining questions, for additional questions by Mr. Krajisnik. I hope you can agree on it. If, finally, that would cause you any problem, then the Chamber will have to decide on the matter and allot time to Defence counsel and to you, Mr. Krajisnik, and the Chamber prefers if you would agree on that with counsel. Mr. Krajisnik, you'd like to address the Chamber? Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have only one question, Your Honour. If the stenographic notes of the session of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were sent to the OTP and have not been translated, can such a document be tendered into evidence? We don't have the capacity to have the entire document translated, and the important discussions are contained in this one particular session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you clearly identify what portions you think are most important to be translated, and then, of course, we'll -- the OTP should be in a position to compare the stenographic notes and the minutes as they were published or at least produced. But please provide us or the OTP, and if there's any problem the Chamber to the extent possible will assist you; provide us with the most relevant parts, and make that clear on a piece of paper so that we can continue. Then we have got 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour will recall there was a matter I wanted to raise when the witness was gone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'd like to do that at this moment, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Going back to this discussion, and I'm talking about page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, since I had a late start on my LiveNote give me two or three words, then I could find --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. "And again that reflects, my concern, Your Honour, about these things, if they have ten days or two weeks ahead of him." This is Mr. Hannis speaking, and that is line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: There is Mr. Hannis at line 8. "Ahead of time. Doesn't appear to support the kinds of questions that were asked and the impression that's given about Mr. Davidovic that troubles me greatly, Your Honour. I think we need to change the process." Then Your Honour indicates, "Yes, I do understand your complaint to be this is approaching a witness in a harassing and intimidating way on insufficient grounds. Before the Chamber can form its opinion on it, of course, we need to inspect all these documents after they have been translated." Now, Your Honour, firstly if there is any suggestion, Your Honour, in relation to harassing and intimidating on insufficient grounds, firstly, Your Honour, as Defence counsel, one can only proceed on the information that is conveyed to you by your investigators. You sift through the material, and you see if there are reasonable grounds to put the questions. Once you've made that determination, you have an obligation as an advocate to put these questions to the witness, and it's an obligation one should never shirk from, regardless of how unpopular it may make you in the world, how unpopular it may make you with the Prosecution, and how unpopular it might make you with the witness. That is an advocate's duty, and I will not have it spoken of lightly in a courtroom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- in that way. And I might add, if I may, I am performing my duty; I am obliged to do my duty, and let's have a look, shall we, at what kind of evidence was brought forward by Mr. Davidovic, in which instance what are we saying, the Defence can't cross-examine unless they produce a document that proves beyond reasonable doubt. All we have to provide, Your Honour, is we are satisfied there is reasonable grounds, and that is the basis. And let's have a look shall we at the kind of evidence that witness was giving. "I heard from somebody that he said that he was sending the money to Mr. Krajisnik." That sort of evidence. Hearsay. Where's the document there that the Prosecution are putting forward? Just out of interest. Let's just turn the page into some other aspects of this particular witness's evidence that this money was being taken to Mr. Krajisnik in Pale. This is what he heard somebody say. That's what's passing for evidence? I don't see a document there. Then we hear about a document that refers to certain things that's signed by Mr. Krajisnik. We never see the document, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, Ms. Loukas, there is a --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there is a difference. Let me just put a hypothetical situation to you. If an investigator says that someone in a village told him that this witness is a rapist, then that might be insufficient to put to a witness, "Aren't you a rapist?" What's the difference with what you said is if a witness appears in this court and if he gives hearsay evidence, first of all, he can be cross-examined on it. To that extent, I mean this Chamber, of course, is not blind for the whole concept of cross- examination, and even if where the case law of this Tribunal does not prohibit it from being admitted, that doesn't mean that the Chamber is not aware that hearsay evidence is certainly not the best evidence. But you compare the information given by a witness during testimony when he has given a solemn declaration that he will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and information given by some unknown source which is put to the witness. You may have noticed that the Chamber didn't stop you when you questioned the witness on these matters. You may also have noticed that, although Mr. Hannis has expressed some concern, that these objections were not such that you're not allowed to put it to the witness. So a clear distinction has to be made. The Chamber does not blame you for performing your duties. At the same time, one could have some concern about the effects of putting quite strong assertions to a witness if finally there would be, and I'm not saying there is not, but if there would be an insufficient basis for such assertions. This is not, I would say, the primary problem for the Defence, but it can be of some concern. Just as it would be of concern to the Chamber whenever a witness would, for whatever reason, feel uncomfortable; not due to being questioned about what is the truth but about any -- be uncomfortable for any reason that should not make him uncomfortable. That's the only thing I'm saying about it. That can be a matter of concern. You were defending your position as Defence counsel. The Chamber fully accepts that you are performing your duties as good as you can. At the same time, if the documentation supporting such questions, which come down to rather strong assertions, is not complete, sometimes caution should be taken there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, I take on board what Your Honour says, but we are in a Tribunal that does not operate on the classic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- systems of evidence, as it were. The Prosecution seems quite content to rely on hearsay, the Tribunal seems quite happy to receive hearsay. Should the Defence information be curtailed in a way that the information that's put forward by the Prosecution and in a way that information is received by the Trial Chamber is not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You, again, make no distinction between sources of information that are part of a testimony given under oath in court and sources of information for, I would say, Defence, but the same would be true for Prosecution preparing activities. The same, if there would be any Defence witness, which would be approached by the Prosecution asserting bad behaviour in the past, in the presence, and if there would be not a sufficiently solid basis for putting that to a witness, then the Chamber would certainly take a similar course where the Prosecution would be invited to show to the Chamber what the basis for this approach of the witness was. So I think it's a matter not specifically for the Defence. It would be true for the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think that what the rule is, in the jurisdiction that I come from ,is that the advocate forms the view that there is a reasonable basis for the matters that are being put, and I acted in accordance with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that enough has been said about it, if you would agree with that, Ms. Loukas. Yes? Mr. Hannis as well.
